prompt: Let $H$ be the orthocenter of the triangle $ABC$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Assume that $H$ lies inside the quadrilateral $BMNC$ and that the circumcircles of triangles $BMH$ and $CNH$ are tangent to each other. The line through $H$ parallel to $BC$ intersects the circumcircles of the triangles $BMH$ and $CNH$ in the points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $F$ be the intersection point of $MK$ and $NL$ and let $J$ be the incenter of triangle $MHN$. Prove that $FJ=FA$.
answer: Proof: an angle chase shows that $MK$ and $NL$ both pass through the circumcentre of $AMN$, so $F$ is that circumcentre; the tangency gives $\angle MHN=180^\circ-2\angle A$, hence $\angle MJN=180^\circ-\angle A$, so $J$ lies on the circle $AMN$ and $FJ=FA$.

solutions.title: $F$ is the circumcentre of $AMN$, and $J$ lies on its circle
solutions.body:
Write $\alpha=\angle BAC$. Since $H$ lies inside $BMNC$, it lies inside triangle $ABC$, so the triangle is acute, and $H$ and $A$ are on opposite sides of $MN$. We use directed angles $\angle(\ell,m)$ between lines, taken modulo $180^\circ$, and orient the plane so that $ABC$ is counterclockwise. Recall: if $XYZ$ is a non-degenerate triangle, then $\angle(XY,XZ)\equiv+\angle YXZ$ if $XYZ$ is counterclockwise and $\equiv-\angle YXZ$ if it is clockwise.

**Step 1: $F$ is the circumcentre $O'$ of triangle $AMN$.** Let $O$ be the circumcentre of $ABC$. The homothety with centre $A$ and ratio $\tfrac12$ maps $B,C,O$ to $M,N,O'$, so $\angle(BO,BC)=\angle(MO',MN)$. In the acute triangle $ABC$ we have $\angle ABH=90^\circ-\alpha=\angle OBC$, so $BH$ and $BO$ are symmetric in the bisector of angle $B$; since a reflection reverses directed angles and swaps $BA$ with $BC$, $\angle(BA,BH)=\angle(BO,BC)$.

The line $KH$ is parallel to $BC$, hence to $MN$, and it is different from $MN$ (it passes through $H\notin MN$); in particular $K\neq M$. As $B,M,H,K$ are concyclic,
$$\angle(MK,MN)=\angle(KM,KH)=\angle(BM,BH)=\angle(BA,BH)=\angle(BO,BC)=\angle(MO',MN).$$
(If $K=H$, the line $KH$ means the tangent at $H$, and the tangent–chord angle gives the same equality.) Hence the lines $MK$ and $MO'$ coincide: $O'\in MK$. In the same way $O'\in NL$. The lines $MK$ and $NL$ are different (otherwise this line would be $MN$, but $K\notin MN$), so $F=O'$ and
$$FA=FM=FN.$$

**Step 2: $\angle MHN=180^\circ-2\alpha$.** Let $t$ be the common tangent of the two circles at $H$. By the tangent–chord angle in circle $BMH$ and in circle $CNH$,
$$\angle(HM,HN)=\angle(HM,t)+\angle(t,HN)=\angle(BM,BH)+\angle(CH,CN)=\angle(BA,BH)+\angle(CH,CA).$$
Because $H$ is inside $ABC$, triangle $BAH$ has the orientation of $BAC$ (clockwise) and triangle $CHA$ the orientation of $CBA$ (clockwise). With $\angle ABH=\angle HCA=90^\circ-\alpha$ this gives
$$\angle(HM,HN)\equiv-(90^\circ-\alpha)-(90^\circ-\alpha)=-(180^\circ-2\alpha).$$
Triangle $AMN$ is counterclockwise and $H$ is on the other side of $MN$, so $HMN$ is clockwise and $\angle(HM,HN)\equiv-\angle MHN$. Thus $\angle MHN\equiv180^\circ-2\alpha\pmod{180^\circ}$, and as both lie strictly between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, $\angle MHN=180^\circ-2\alpha$.

**Step 3: $J$ lies on the circle $AMN$.** For the incentre $J$ of $MHN$,
$$\angle MJN=180^\circ-\tfrac12(\angle HMN+\angle HNM)=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle MHN=180^\circ-\alpha .$$
$J$ lies inside triangle $MHN$, so it is on the opposite side of $MN$ from $A$. Since $\angle MAN+\angle MJN=180^\circ$, the quadrilateral $AMJN$ is cyclic. So $J$ lies on the circumcircle of $AMN$, whose centre is $F$ by Step 1. Therefore $FJ=FA$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be given by
$$f(x)=\frac1x+\frac1{x-2}+\frac1{x-4}+\cdots+\frac1{x-2018}$$
and
$$g(x)=\frac1{x-1}+\frac1{x-3}+\frac1{x-5}+\cdots+\frac1{x-2017}.$$
Prove that
$$|f(x)-g(x)|>2$$
for any non-integer real number $x$ satisfying $0<x<2018$.
answer: Proof: with $d=g-f$, the symmetry $d(2018-x)=-d(x)$ reduces to $x\in(2m-1,2m)$; $d(x+2)>d(x)$ reduces further to $1<x<2$, where pairing terms gives $d(x)>\frac1{(x-1)(2-x)}-\frac3{x(3-x)}>4-\frac32>2$.

solutions.title: Symmetry, monotone shift and pairing
solutions.body:
Let $d(x)=g(x)-f(x)$.

**Symmetry.** Replacing $x$ by $2018-x$ gives $\frac1{2018-x-2k}=-\frac1{x-(2018-2k)}$, and $2018-2k$ runs over the same set $\{0,2,\dots,2018\}$ as $2k$; so $f(2018-x)=-f(x)$, and likewise $g(2018-x)=-g(x)$ (the odd numbers $1,\dots,2017$ are also mapped to themselves). Hence $d(2018-x)=-d(x)$. A non-integer $x\in(0,2018)$ lies in some interval $(2m-1,2m)$ or $(2m,2m+1)$; in the second case $2018-x\in(2m'-1,2m')$ with $m'=1009-m$. So it suffices to prove
$$d(x)>2\qquad\text{for } 2m-1<x<2m,\ 1\le m\le1009 .$$

**Shifting by $2$.** Shifting the indices,
$$d(x+2)-d(x)=\Big(\frac1{x+1}-\frac1{x+2}\Big)+\Big(\frac1{x-2018}-\frac1{x-2017}\Big).$$
For $0<x<2016$ the first bracket is positive, and since $x-2018<x-2017<0$ the second is positive too. So $d(x+2)>d(x)$, and by induction $d(x+2m-2)\ge d(x)$ for $1<x<2$. It therefore suffices to treat $1<x<2$.

**The case $1<x<2$.** Group the terms as
$$d(x)=\Big(\frac1{x-1}-\frac1{x-2}\Big)+\Big(\frac1{x-3}-\frac1x\Big)+\sum_{i=2}^{1008}\Big(\frac1{x-2i-1}-\frac1{x-2i}\Big)-\frac1{x-2018}.$$
For $i\ge2$ we have $x-2i-1<x-2i<0$, so each bracket in the sum is positive; and $-\frac1{x-2018}>0$. Hence
$$d(x)>\frac1{x-1}+\frac1{2-x}+\frac1{x-3}-\frac1x=\frac1{(x-1)(2-x)}-\frac3{x(3-x)} .$$
Now $(x-1)(2-x)=\tfrac14-(x-\tfrac32)^2\le\tfrac14$, so the first fraction is at least $4$; and $x(3-x)=\tfrac94-(x-\tfrac32)^2>\tfrac94-\tfrac14=2$, so the second is less than $\tfrac32$. Thus $d(x)>4-\tfrac32>2$.

Therefore $|f(x)-g(x)|=|d(x)|>2$ for every non-integer $x\in(0,2018)$. ∎

prompt:
A collection of $n$ squares on the plane is called *tri-connected* if the following criteria are satisfied:

(i) All the squares are congruent.

(ii) If two squares have a point $P$ in common, then $P$ is a vertex of each of the squares.

(iii) Each square touches exactly three other squares.

How many positive integers $n$ are there with $2018\le n\le3018$, such that there exists a collection of $n$ squares that is tri-connected?

solutions.title: Parity, then a necklace of small blocks
solutions.body:
The answer is the number of even $n$ in $[2018,3018]$, namely $\frac{3018-2018}{2}+1=501$.

**$n$ must be even.** Counting ordered pairs of touching squares, each of the $n$ squares contributes $3$, giving $3n$; but every touching pair is counted twice. So $3n$ is even, hence $n$ is even.

**Every even $n\in[2018,3018]$ works.** Use unit squares and two building blocks ("beads"). Each bead has two marked *ports* $Q$ and $P$; each port is a vertex of exactly one square of the bead, and that square has exactly two neighbours inside the bead, while every other square of the bead has exactly three. Inside a bead, squares meet only at common vertices.

*Bead $\mathcal A$ (4 squares).* Take the equilateral triangle $(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2),(-\tfrac12,0),(\tfrac12,0)$ and erect unit squares outward on its three sides; add the square $t$ with vertices $T,\ T+(\tfrac{\sqrt2}2,\tfrac{\sqrt2}2),\ T+(0,\sqrt2),\ T+(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2,\tfrac{\sqrt2}2)$, where $T=(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)$. Around $T$ the triangle occupies directions $[240^\circ,300^\circ]$, the two side squares $[-60^\circ,30^\circ]$ and $[150^\circ,240^\circ]$, and $t$ occupies $[45^\circ,135^\circ]$; so these squares meet only at $T$. The two side squares at $T$ touch each other, $t$, and the bottom square; the bottom square and $t$ have two neighbours each. Ports: $Q=T+(0,\sqrt2)$ (on $t$) and $P=(\tfrac12,-1)$ (on the bottom square).

*Bead $\mathcal B$ (6 squares).* Let $c=\frac{1+\sqrt3}2$. Take the square with vertices $(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2),(-\tfrac12,0),(-c,\tfrac12),(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2,c)$, its mirror images in the $y$-axis, in the $x$-axis and in the origin (four squares forming a ring around the origin, consecutive ones sharing the vertices $(0,\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)$, $(\pm\tfrac12,0)$), plus the axis-parallel squares $[-c-1,-c]\times[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$ and $[c,c+1]\times[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$, which touch the two ring squares on their side at $(\pm c,\pm\tfrac12)$. Each ring square has three neighbours, the two end squares two. Ports: $Q=(-c-1,\tfrac12)$, $P=(c+1,-\tfrac12)$.

A direct computation from these coordinates verifies the properties claimed above, and also the following: with $u=\frac{P-Q}{|P-Q|}$, every vertex $v\ne Q$ of the bead satisfies $\angle(v-Q,u)<82^\circ$ and every vertex $v\ne P$ satisfies $\angle(P-v,u)<82^\circ$. (The worst case is $\approx81.3^\circ$, at $P$ of bead $\mathcal A$.) As the squares are convex hulls of their vertices and the cone of directions within $82^\circ$ of $u$ is convex, the same holds for every point of the bead other than $Q$, resp. $P$. The port distances are $d_{\mathcal A}=|PQ|\approx3.318$ and $d_{\mathcal B}\approx4.837$.

*The necklace.* Given beads $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_m$ with port distances $d_j$, choose $\rho$ with $\sum_j2\arcsin\frac{d_j}{2\rho}=2\pi$ (the left side decreases continuously to $0$ as $\rho\to\infty$, and exceeds $2\pi$ at $\rho=\max d_j/2$ when $m$ is large). Put points $X_0,X_1,\dots,X_m=X_0$ on the circle of radius $\rho$ about $C$ with $\angle X_{j-1}CX_j=\theta_j=2\arcsin\frac{d_j}{2\rho}$, so $|X_{j-1}X_j|=d_j$, and place $\beta_j$ by a rigid motion with $Q\mapsto X_{j-1}$, $P\mapsto X_j$. At $X_{j-1}$, the ray towards $C$ makes the angle $90^\circ-\frac{\theta_j}2$ with the chord $X_{j-1}X_j$, and so does the ray $X_jC$ at $X_j$. If $\frac{\theta_j}2<8^\circ$, the angle condition above puts every point of $\beta_j$ other than its ports strictly inside the open sector $X_{j-1}CX_j$. The open sectors are disjoint, so two different beads can meet only at a common port: $\beta_j$ and $\beta_{j+1}$ meet exactly at $X_j$, which is a vertex of one end square of each, and non-consecutive beads do not meet at all. Every end square gains exactly one neighbour, so every square has exactly three neighbours, and all contacts are at common vertices: the necklace is tri-connected.

*Sizes.* For even $n\in[2018,3018]$: if $4\mid n$ use $n/4\ge505$ copies of $\mathcal A$; otherwise $n\equiv2\pmod4$ and we use $\frac{n-6}4\ge503$ copies of $\mathcal A$ and one $\mathcal B$. In both cases $m\ge504$. The copies of $\mathcal A$ all have the same angle $\theta_{\mathcal A}$, and $(m-1)\theta_{\mathcal A}<2\pi$, so $\theta_{\mathcal A}<\frac{2\pi}{503}<1^\circ$. For $\mathcal B$, $\sin\frac{\theta_{\mathcal B}}2=\frac{d_{\mathcal B}}{d_{\mathcal A}}\sin\frac{\theta_{\mathcal A}}2<1.5\sin\frac{\theta_{\mathcal A}}2<0.02$, so $\frac{\theta_{\mathcal B}}2<2^\circ$. The condition $\frac{\theta_j}2<8^\circ$ holds for all beads, so every even $n$ in the range is realised.

Hence the answer is $\mathbf{501}$. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle. From the vertex $A$ we draw a ray towards the interior of the triangle such that the ray reaches one of the sides of the triangle. When the ray reaches a side, it then bounces off following the law of reflection, that is, if it arrives with a directed angle $\alpha$, it leaves with a directed angle $180^\circ-\alpha$. After $n$ bounces, the ray returns to $A$ without ever landing on any of the other two vertices. Find all possible values of $n$.

solutions.title: Unfold into the triangular lattice
solutions.body:
**Unfolding.** Reflecting the triangle in the side that the ray hits, again and again, straightens the path into a ray from $A$ through the tiling of the plane by copies of $ABC$. Put $A=0$, $\vec{AB}=e_1$, $\vec{AC}=e_2$; the lattice points are $ae_1+be_2=(a,b)$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Z$, and the tiling lines are $a=\text{const}$, $b=\text{const}$, $a+b=\text{const}$ (integers).

Label $(a,b)$ by $a-b\bmod3$; then $A,B,C$ get $0,1,2$. Every tile has vertices $(a,b),(a+1,b),(a,b+1)$ or $(a+1,b),(a,b+1),(a+1,b+1)$, which carry three different labels. When the tile is reflected in an edge, the new vertex gets the label not used on that edge, i.e. the label of the vertex it is the image of. By induction along the tiles crossed, the image of $A$ in each copy is a lattice point with label $0$, and similarly for $B$ (label $1$) and $C$ (label $2$).

The ray starts into the interior, so its direction is strictly between $e_1$ and $e_2$. The billiard reaches a vertex exactly when the straight ray meets a lattice point, and that vertex is $A$ exactly when the lattice point has label $0$. So the ray returns to $A$ without first landing on $B$ or $C$ if and only if the first lattice point on the straight ray is some $(a,b)$ with
$$a,b\ge1,\qquad \gcd(a,b)=1,\qquad a\equiv b\pmod3$$
(the first lattice point on the ray towards $(a,b)$ is $(a,b)/\gcd(a,b)$). The open segment from $0$ to $(a,b)$ crosses $a-1$ lines $a=\text{const}$, $b-1$ lines $b=\text{const}$ and $a+b-1$ lines $a+b=\text{const}$. Since there is no lattice point on it, no two crossings coincide, and each crossing is one bounce. So
$$n=2(a+b)-3 .$$

**Which $n$ occur.** Put $s=a+b\ge2$. If $3\mid s$ then $a\equiv b$ gives $3\mid 2a$, so $3$ divides $a$ and $b$, contradicting $\gcd(a,b)=1$. So $3\nmid s$, and the conditions become: some $a$ with $1\le a\le s-1$, $a\equiv-s\pmod3$ and $\gcd(a,s)=1$. In particular $n=2s-3$ is odd and not divisible by $3$, so $n\equiv1,5\pmod6$.

* $s\equiv2\pmod3$, i.e. $n=6j+1$: $a=1$ works. All $n\equiv1\pmod 6$ occur.
* $s\equiv1\pmod3$, i.e. $n\equiv5\pmod6$; we need $a\equiv2\pmod3$.
  * $s$ odd, $s=6k+1$ with $k\ge1$ ($n=12k-1$): $a=2$ works.
  * $s=6k+4$ ($n=12k+5$), $k$ even, $k\ge2$: take $a=3k-1$. It is $\equiv2\pmod3$, odd, $1\le a\le s-1$, and $\gcd(3k-1,6k+4)=\gcd(3k-1,6)=1$.
  * $s=6k+4$, $k$ odd, $k\ge3$: take $a=3k-4$. It is $\equiv2\pmod3$, odd, $1\le a\le s-1$, and $\gcd(3k-4,6k+4)=\gcd(3k-4,12)=1$.
  * $s=4$ ($n=5$): the only candidate is $a=2$, but $\gcd(2,4)=2$. $s=10$ ($n=17$): the candidates $a=2,5,8$ all share a factor with $10$. So $5$ and $17$ are impossible.

**Answer:** exactly the positive integers $n\equiv1$ or $5\pmod6$ other than $5$ and $17$. ∎

prompt: Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for all real numbers $s$ and $t$, if $P(s)$ and $P(t)$ are both integers, then $P(st)$ is also an integer.

solutions.title: Irreducibility of $P(x)-p$
solutions.body:
**These work.** If $P=\pm x^n+k$ and $P(s),P(t)\in\mathbb Z$, then $s^n,t^n\in\mathbb Z$, so $(st)^n=s^nt^n\in\mathbb Z$ and $P(st)\in\mathbb Z$.

**Nothing else works.** If $P$ has the property, so does $\pm P+k$ for every integer $k$. Constant polynomials are on the list, so let $n=\deg P\ge1$ and normalise to $a_n>0$, $P(0)=0$:
$$P(x)=a_nx^n+\dots+a_1x .$$
We show $P(x)=x^n$.

Choose a prime $p>\sum_{i=1}^n|a_i|$. Since $P(0)=0<p$ and $P(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$, there is a real $t$ with $P(t)=p$. Also $P(2)\in\mathbb Z$, so by hypothesis $q:=P(2t)$ is an integer.

*$P(x)-p$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$.* Suppose $P(x)-p=F(x)G(x)$ with non-constant $F,G$; by Gauss's lemma we may take $F,G\in\mathbb Z[x]$. Then $F(0)G(0)=-p$, so one of them, say $F$, has $F(0)=\pm1$. If $c$ is the leading coefficient of $F$, the complex roots of $F$ have product of absolute value $1/|c|\le1$, so $F$ has a root $r$ with $|r|\le1$. Then $P(r)=p$, but $|P(r)|\le\sum|a_i||r|^i\le\sum|a_i|<p$, a contradiction.

*Comparing polynomials.* $t$ is a root of the irreducible polynomial $P(x)-p$, which is therefore (up to a constant factor) the minimal polynomial of $t$ over $\mathbb Q$. Since $t$ is also a root of $P(2x)-q\in\mathbb Q[x]$, the polynomial $P(x)-p$ divides $P(2x)-q$. They have the same degree, so $P(2x)-q=\lambda(P(x)-p)$; the leading coefficients give $\lambda=2^n$. Comparing the coefficients of $x^i$ for $1\le i<n$: $2^ia_i=2^na_i$, so $a_i=0$. Hence $P(x)=a_nx^n$.

*Leading coefficient.* Let $s=a_n^{-1/n}>0$. Then $P(s)=1$, so $P(s\cdot s)=a_ns^{2n}=\frac1{a_n}$ must be an integer, which forces $a_n=1$.

Undoing the normalisation, $P(x)=\pm x^n+k$. ∎
